title: Ask again (2:9)
hook: if refused, return with three friends, up to three times
tomorrow: and when you're the one asked, how fast should you say yes?

segments.voice: Yesterday: repair first. Wrongs between people wait until you give back what's owed and win the person over. But winning someone over takes two.

"Not yet." Two words on a lock screen, after the sorry you worked up the nerve to send. What if you ask, and they say no? One instinct says give up, you tried. Another says keep asking, tonight, until they cave. Maimonides has a third answer, and it's oddly precise. One question for today: how many times do you have to ask?
screen: `NOT YET.` → `GIVE UP, OR KEEP PUSHING?` → `HOW MANY TIMES?`

segments.voice: In the same halakhah as yesterday, he writes: if the one you wronged doesn't want to forgive, bring three of their friends, and go to them together, and ask. If they refuse, come back a second time, and a third. If they still refuse, you may leave them be. And then the line that turns the whole thing around: the one who won't forgive is now the one in the wrong. There's one exception. If the person is your teacher, Maimonides says, go even a thousand times. Notice what the friends are for. Not a mob. People the other person trusts, who can say: this is real, you can open the door. And notice the limit. Asking is a duty, but it isn't a siege. Now a neighbor. Christians read a strikingly similar step in the Gospel of Matthew. "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone." And if he won't hear, "take with thee one or two more." Both traditions bring in a few trusted people when two alone get stuck, so a broken thing doesn't stay broken out of pride. The honest difference: in Matthew, the one who goes is the one who was wronged. In Maimonides, it's the one who did the wrong, going to ask. Same few friends, walking in from opposite sides of the fight.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS, THREE TIMES.` · `THE REFUSER NOW CARRIES IT.` · `MATTHEW: ONE OR TWO MORE.` · `FROM OPPOSITE SIDES.` · then, large: `ASK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one door that closed on you after you asked. Without forcing anything, ask yourself who the other person trusts, and what a calmer second ask might sound like. Hold that picture until the bell.
screen: `ONE CLOSED DOOR.` · `WHO DO THEY TRUST?` · `A CALMER SECOND ASK.`

segments.voice: Ask again: Maimonides' rule when forgiveness is refused. Return with three friends, up to three times; then the refusal is theirs to carry.
Hold onto this: ask again, but not tonight, not alone, and not forever. Day fifteen forty-six, still asking.

screen: `DAY 1546 COUNTS.` → `MAIMONIDES, THE LAWS OF RETURN · 9 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: AND WHEN YOU'RE THE ONE ASKED, HOW FAST SHOULD YOU SAY YES?`

howItsDone: Jewish law treats asking forgiveness as an obligation with limits: the one who did wrong asks, returns with others if refused, and after three sincere tries is no longer bound to keep asking (Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:9).

chat.meaning: Maimonides: if refused, ask again, with trusted people, up to three times. A duty with limits, not a siege.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Matthew 18:15-16 as a neighbor tradition's own words; the shared step is bringing in a few trusted people; the honest difference is direction (in Matthew the wronged goes; in Maimonides the wrongdoer). Christian readers interpret Matthew 18 variously (church discipline, reconciliation); the voice says only what the verse says. Confirm fair framing, no ranking.
Matthew 18:15 in KJV begins 'Moreover if thy brother'; the quotation starts at 'If'. Confirm.
Yoma 87a: the source behind the 'three' (three rows of three people, three times); summarized only in sources. Confirm.
'The Gospel of Matthew' glossed as the first book of the New Testament (canonical order). Confirm.
